lead: Utah homes take water damage from frozen pipes, snowmelt and desert flash floods. DryFlare helps owners from Salt Lake City to Provo and St. George dry out fast.
risk: frozen pipes, spring snowmelt flooding and flash floods in the south
why: Big snow years bring spring floods. After the record snowpack of 2023, runoff flooded streets and basements along the Wasatch Front. Many homes there have basements, and many are finished. A burst pipe in winter or a failed sump pump can flood a whole lower level.

Southern Utah is a different story. Summer storms send flash floods through slot canyons and washes around St. George. Statewide, hard water wears out water heaters and fittings early. Colorado and Idaho share Utah's winter risks, and Nevada shares the desert storms.
image_alt: Frost-covered water valve in winter sun
image_caption: Burst pipes in finished basements are a common winter claim along the Wasatch Front.
problems: Salt Lake, Utah and Davis counties
tips: Shut off and drain outside spigots before winter.
Replace water heaters at the end of their rated life; hard water shortens it.
In St. George, never enter a wash during a storm.
Add a leak sensor near the water heater and washer.
insurance: Utah policies cover sudden pipe bursts, but flooding from snowmelt runoff needs a separate flood policy.

faq.q: How long does it take to dry a finished basement in Utah?
faq.a: Usually three to five days once wet carpet pad and drywall are removed. Utah's dry air helps, but concrete and framing still need dehumidifiers. Crews check moisture readings before rebuilding.

licensing_faq: Yes. Utah's Division of Professional Licensing (DOPL) licenses contractors, and most construction work needs a licensed contractor.
